title: Hangover Gummies: Do They Work? PartySmart, Undo and DHM Compared
excerpt: Do hangover gummies work? An honest look at the ingredients in DHM, PartySmart, and Undo gummies, the drawbacks of the gummy format, and how to pick one.
metaDescription: Do hangover gummies work? An honest look at DHM, PartySmart, and Undo gummies: ingredients, evidence, sugar, dose problems, and how to choose one.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** hangover gummies are a convenient, tasty way to take the same ingredients you'd find in hangover pills and drinks, but the gummy format itself doesn't make them work any better. Some of their ingredients, such as DHM, prickly pear, and L-cysteine, have early research behind them. Others, like most vitamin and electrolyte blends, are mainly there for marketing. There is no good evidence that any gummy prevents hangovers reliably, and none of them lowers your blood alcohol or makes it safe to drive. What matters most is what's inside each gummy and how much of it, and that's exactly where gummies tend to fall short.

**The quick rules:** Read the label, not the front of the bag. Check how many gummies make one serving, how much of each active ingredient that serving contains, and how much sugar comes with it. Be wary of "proprietary blends" that hide the amounts. Store them away from kids and pets, because they look and taste like candy. And if you take prescription medication, especially sedatives, blood thinners, or diabetes medicine, check with a pharmacist before adding an herbal blend.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article reviews general research and product labels. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Get medical help right away if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and no supplement treats it. Call 911 (or your local emergency number). If a child or pet eats gummies that weren't meant for them, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) or your vet.

## What Hangover Gummies Are

Hangover gummies are chewable supplements sold to take before, during, or after drinking. They sit in the same category as hangover pills, powders, patches, and shots. The difference is the delivery method: a gelatin or pectin base, flavoring, and sweetener wrapped around a small amount of active ingredients.

Most products on the market fall into a few groups:

- **DHM gummies.** These are built around dihydromyricetin (DHM), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree (Hovenia dulcis). This is the ingredient with the most research specific to alcohol.
- **Herbal blend gummies.** These combine several plant extracts, often from Ayurvedic or traditional Asian medicine, such as amla (Indian gooseberry), chicory, kudzu, milk thistle, or ginger. Himalaya's PartySmart line is the best-known example of this approach.
- **Vitamin and electrolyte gummies.** These lean on B vitamins, vitamin C, zinc, and small amounts of electrolytes. They're the easiest to make taste good and the hardest to justify on evidence.
- **Combination gummies.** Many brands mix all of the above, sometimes adding L-cysteine, N-acetylcysteine (NAC), prickly pear, or ginseng.

Brand names you'll see when searching include PartySmart, Undo, and a long list of DHM gummies from supplement companies and private-label sellers. Formulas in this market change often, so the label on the bag in front of you is the only reliable source for what you're getting.

## Do Hangover Gummies Work?

The fair answer is: some ingredients have promising early evidence, the products themselves have very little, and the gummy format adds its own limits.

When researchers have looked at hangover remedies as a whole, the picture is thin. A 2022 systematic review in the journal *Addiction* looked at placebo-controlled trials of hangover treatments and judged the evidence for all of them to be very low quality. Studies tended to be small, short, and often funded by the companies selling the product. That review didn't find that nothing works. It found that nothing has been tested well enough to say for sure.

There's another layer. Most studies test an ingredient, usually as a capsule or extract at a specific dose. Very few test a specific branded gummy. So when a gummy brand says its ingredients are "clinically studied," that usually means someone, somewhere, studied one of the ingredients, often at a different dose and in a different form.

Here's how the common gummy ingredients stack up.

### DHM (dihydromyricetin)

DHM is the most researched hangover-specific ingredient. A well-known 2012 study in the *Journal of Neuroscience* found that DHM reduced alcohol intoxication and some withdrawal signs in rats, apparently by acting on GABA receptors in the brain. Later lab and animal studies suggest it may help the body process alcohol and its toxic by-product, acetaldehyde, and may support liver health. A 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease found improvements in some liver markers. Human trials looking directly at hangovers are still small and limited.

It's promising, not proven. If you want to know more, our [honest review of whether DHM works](/never-hungover/does-dhm-work-honest-science-review-2025) goes through the studies one by one.

### Prickly pear (Opuntia ficus-indica)

A 2004 study in the *Archives of Internal Medicine* gave volunteers prickly pear extract or a placebo before drinking. The prickly pear group reported less nausea, dry mouth, and loss of appetite, though the overall hangover score didn't change much. That's one small study, but it's a real one, and it's why you'll see prickly pear in a lot of formulas.

### L-cysteine and NAC

L-cysteine is an amino acid your body uses to make glutathione, an antioxidant that helps clear acetaldehyde. A small Finnish study published in 2020 reported that people who took L-cysteine had milder hangover symptoms than those taking placebo. NAC is a close relative. Both are promising for the same reason, and both need bigger studies.

### Herbal blends (amla, chicory, kudzu, milk thistle)

Himalaya says its PartySmart formula is based on traditional herbs and points to its own research showing lower acetaldehyde after drinking. That kind of company-run research is a reasonable starting point, but we couldn't find large independent trials of the product. Milk thistle has more research behind it for liver health generally, with mixed results in people. Kudzu has a small amount of research suggesting it may affect how much people drink, which is a different question from whether it eases a hangover.

### Ginger

Ginger has decent evidence for easing nausea in other settings, such as pregnancy and motion sickness. It hasn't been studied much for hangovers specifically, but if nausea is your main problem, it's a sensible ingredient. The catch is that a gummy usually holds only a small amount.

### B vitamins and zinc

Drinking can lower levels of some B vitamins over time, and a Dutch survey study linked higher dietary intake of zinc and vitamin B3 with less severe hangovers. That's an association from people's normal diets, not proof that a gummy will help. If you eat reasonably well, topping up the night you drink is unlikely to make a noticeable difference. Our guide to [vitamins for a hangover](/never-hungover/vitamins-for-hangover) covers which ones have any case.

### Electrolytes

Alcohol makes you urinate more, so losing fluid is part of why you feel rough. But research has generally found that hangover severity doesn't track closely with electrolyte levels in the blood, and a gummy holds only a tiny fraction of the sodium and potassium in an electrolyte drink. Water and food do far more. If hydration is your main goal, our comparison of [electrolyte drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) is a better place to start.

## The Problems With the Gummy Format

Gummies are pleasant to take, and for some people that's the whole point: if you won't swallow capsules, a gummy you'll actually take beats a pill sitting in a drawer. But the format has real drawbacks that are worth knowing before you buy.

### There isn't much room for the active ingredient

A typical gummy weighs a few grams, and most of that is the gummy base, sugar, and flavoring. That limits how much active ingredient fits inside. DHM studies and most DHM capsules use doses in the range of several hundred milligrams up to around 1,000 mg. Packing that much into one gummy is hard, and DHM tastes bitter, which makes it harder still. So many DHM gummies either contain less per serving or ask you to eat two, three, or four gummies at a time. Always do the math: dose per gummy times gummies per serving.

### Label accuracy is a known weak spot

Gummies are harder to manufacture accurately than capsules or tablets. Ingredients can degrade with heat and moisture, and getting an even amount into every gummy is tricky. A 2023 study in *JAMA* tested melatonin gummies sold in the US and found that the actual amount in most products didn't match the label, ranging from well below to several times above what was listed. That study was about melatonin, not hangover products, but it shows the general problem. Look for brands that use third-party testing (such as USP, NSF, or a published certificate of analysis), because that's the only way to know the label is close to the truth.

### Sugar adds up

Many gummies contain a few grams of sugar each. That's not much on its own, but a three- or four-gummy serving taken on top of cocktails or mixers adds up. If you're watching sugar or have diabetes, look for sugar-free versions, and be aware that those often use sugar alcohols, which can upset some stomachs.

### Heat and storage

Gummies melt, stick together, and can lose potency when left in a hot car or bag. That matters for the exact situations people buy them for: festivals, beach trips, and travel. Capsules hold up better.

### They cost more per dose

Because of the lower dose per piece and the more complex manufacturing, gummies usually cost more per effective serving than capsules with the same ingredient. That's not a dealbreaker if the format is the reason you'll actually take them, but it's worth checking the price per serving rather than per bag.

### They look like candy

This is a genuine safety point. Kids can mistake supplement gummies for sweets, and some sugar-free gummies use xylitol, which is toxic to dogs even in small amounts. Keep them out of reach the same way you would any medicine.

## A Closer Look at the Brands People Search For

We don't sell either of these brands, and we have no affiliate relationship with them. Here's what you should know.

### PartySmart (Himalaya)

**What it is:** A herbal hangover supplement from Himalaya Wellness, an Indian company with a long history in Ayurvedic products. PartySmart has been sold as a capsule for years, and the brand has also offered chewable and gummy versions. The formula centers on a blend of traditional herbs.

**Pros:**
- Made by a large, established manufacturer rather than a pop-up brand.
- Usually affordable per serving compared with many DHM products.
- One serving is meant to be taken around drinking, which is easy to remember.

**Cons:**
- The main evidence comes from the company's own research. We couldn't find large, independent, peer-reviewed trials of the finished product.
- Herbal blends can be harder to judge, because the label may not spell out exactly how much of each herb is included.
- Herbs like andrographis and others in Ayurvedic formulas can interact with some medicines. If you take prescription drugs, ask a pharmacist.

**Who it suits:** People who want an inexpensive, simple product and are comfortable with herbal remedies that have modest evidence.

### Undo

**What it is:** Undo is one of the names that comes up most when people search for hangover gummies. Like many brands in this space, it markets a blend of vitamins and plant extracts in a gummy aimed at the morning after.

**Pros:**
- Easy to take and convenient to carry.
- A gummy format may suit people who dislike swallowing pills.

**Cons:**
- We couldn't find a published, independent trial of the Undo product itself.
- As with most gummies, check how much of each active ingredient you get per serving, and whether the brand publishes third-party test results.
- Check the sugar and sweetener on the label, especially if you need to limit either.

**Who it suits:** People who value convenience and taste, and who treat it as one small part of a bigger plan rather than the plan itself.

### Generic DHM gummies

**What they are:** A growing number of supplement sellers offer DHM gummies, often combined with electrolytes, B vitamins, or milk thistle.

**Pros:**
- Built around the ingredient with the most alcohol-specific research.
- Easy to compare with DHM capsules, since the key number is simply milligrams of DHM per serving.

**Cons:**
- DHM per gummy is often low, and servings may require several gummies.
- Label accuracy varies widely between sellers. Third-party testing matters a lot here.
- Cost per milligram of DHM is usually higher than in capsules.

**Who they suit:** People who want to try DHM and won't take capsules.

## Gummies vs Pills vs Drinks: Which Format Makes Sense?

There's no single best format. Each trades something off.

| Format | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Gummies | Pleasant to take, easy to carry, good for people who dislike pills | Lower dose per piece, sugar, heat-sensitive, more label-accuracy problems, higher cost per dose |
| Capsules and tablets | Highest dose in the smallest size, stable, cheapest per dose, easiest to verify | Some people dislike swallowing pills; need to remember water |
| Drinks and shots | Come with fluid, often electrolytes, easy to take before bed | Bulky to carry, often pricier, ingredient amounts may be hidden in blends |
| Patches | Very convenient | Little or no evidence that hangover ingredients absorb through the skin in useful amounts |

If your aim is simply to try an ingredient like DHM and see if it does anything for you, capsules are usually the more reliable and cheaper test. Our comparison of [DHM supplement forms](/never-hungover/dhm-product-forms-absorption-comparison-2025) covers absorption and cost across formats, our roundup of [hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) covers the drink options, and our guide to [hangover patches](/never-hungover/do-hangover-patches-work) looks at whether patches deliver anything useful.

## How to Choose a Hangover Gummy

If you prefer gummies, here's a simple checklist to separate the decent products from the candy with a health claim attached.

1. **Find the real dose.** Look at the Supplement Facts panel. How many gummies is one serving, and how many milligrams of each active ingredient does that serving give you?
2. **Avoid hidden amounts.** A "proprietary blend" lists the total weight but not how much of each ingredient. That makes it impossible to compare with research doses.
3. **Look for third-party testing.** A USP or NSF seal, or a certificate of analysis you can actually view, is the best sign the label is accurate.
4. **Check sugar and sweeteners.** Compare grams of sugar per serving, and note sugar alcohols or xylitol if you have pets or a sensitive stomach.
5. **Be skeptical of big promises.** Claims like "no more hangovers" or "detox your liver overnight" are red flags. Responsible brands use careful wording.
6. **Check the price per serving.** Divide the price by the number of servings, not the number of gummies.
7. **Think about your medication.** Herbal blends are more likely than single ingredients to interact with prescriptions.

## How to Use Hangover Gummies (If You Do)

Follow the label, but a few general points apply to almost every product:

- **Timing usually matters more than people think.** Most DHM-based products suggest taking a serving while drinking or before bed. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers timing and amounts in more detail.
- **Take them with water.** A gummy doesn't hydrate you. Pair it with a full glass of water, and alternate water with alcohol through the night.
- **Eat.** Drinking on a full stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood. Food does more for your morning than any supplement.
- **Don't double up to compensate.** If one serving didn't seem to help, eating the whole bag next time won't either, and it can push vitamins like B6 or herbal extracts to levels you don't want.
- **Don't mix with sleep aids casually.** Some people pair hangover gummies with melatonin gummies. Melatonin and alcohol can both make you drowsy, so read our guide to [melatonin and alcohol](/never-hungover/melatonin-and-alcohol) before combining them.

## Safety and Side Effects

Most hangover gummies are well tolerated by healthy adults when taken as directed. The most common complaints are mild: stomach upset, bloating, or loose stools, especially from sugar alcohols. A few points deserve more care:

- **Medication interactions.** Herbal ingredients like kudzu, milk thistle, ginseng, and some Ayurvedic herbs can interact with blood thinners, diabetes medicines, blood pressure drugs, and others. DHM has limited interaction data in people. If you take prescription medicine, talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using any hangover supplement. Our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers what's known.
- **Pregnancy and breastfeeding.** These products haven't been studied for safety in pregnancy, and alcohol itself should be avoided.
- **Liver conditions.** If you have liver disease, talk to your doctor before taking supplements marketed for the liver, and be honest about how much you drink.
- **They don't make you sober.** No gummy lowers your blood alcohol level or speeds up how fast you sober up enough to drive. Plan a safe ride home regardless.

## When a Hangover Is Something More

A rough morning after a night out is usually just that. But some symptoms point to something that needs medical attention, not a supplement.

> **When to see a doctor or get help.** Call 911 or get emergency care if someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning: confusion, passing out and being hard to wake, repeated vomiting, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or pale, bluish, or cold skin. See a doctor soon if you vomit blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, have severe stomach pain, notice yellowing of your skin or eyes, or still feel very unwell more than a day after drinking. If you notice shaking, sweating, anxiety, or a racing heart when you go without a drink, especially after drinking heavily for several days in a row, say so plainly to a doctor. Those can be withdrawal signals, and they're worth checking rather than treating as a bad hangover.

## The Smarter Strategy: What Actually Helps

Hangover gummies are at best a small add-on. The things with the strongest evidence are free:

- **Drink less, and drink slower.** The amount of alcohol is the biggest predictor of how bad a hangover will be.
- **Eat before and while you drink.**
- **Alternate alcohol with water.**
- **Choose clearer drinks.** Darker drinks like bourbon and red wine contain more congeners, by-products of fermentation that have been linked to worse hangovers.
- **Protect your sleep.** Alcohol disrupts sleep quality, which is a big part of feeling wrecked the next day.

Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through each of these, and our honest look at [whether hangover pills actually work](/never-hungover/do-hangover-pills-actually-work) covers the wider supplement market.

## A Simpler Way to Try DHM

If what draws you to hangover gummies is DHM, capsules give you a clearly labeled dose at a lower cost per serving. [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) lists 1,000 mg of DHM per serving at well under a dollar a serving, which makes it an inexpensive way to find out whether DHM does anything for you. If you'd rather have a combination formula, [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) pairs DHM with L-cysteine, milk thistle, prickly pear, and electrolytes. Our [best hangover pills guide](/never-hungover/best-hangover-pills) compares more options. (We earn a small commission if you buy through these links, at no extra cost to you.)

Like any gummy, neither is a cure, and there is no good evidence that any supplement prevents hangovers for everyone. Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medicine.

## The Bottom Line

Hangover gummies are a format, not a breakthrough. The ingredients inside them range from promising (DHM, prickly pear, L-cysteine) to mostly marketing (electrolyte and vitamin blends at tiny doses). Gummies tend to deliver less of the active ingredient per piece, carry extra sugar, cost more per dose, and have a weaker track record for label accuracy than capsules. If you love the format and you'll actually take them, choose a third-party tested product with a clear dose. If you just want to test whether an ingredient helps you, capsules are the simpler, cheaper experiment. And whatever you take, water, food, and fewer drinks will do more for your morning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do hangover gummies actually work?**

Some of their ingredients have early evidence, but the products themselves have very little. DHM, prickly pear, and L-cysteine have small studies suggesting they may ease some hangover symptoms. Vitamin and electrolyte gummies have much weaker support. There is no good evidence that any gummy prevents hangovers reliably, and the gummy format often delivers less of the active ingredient than a capsule.

**Are hangover gummies better than hangover pills?**

Not in terms of effectiveness. Gummies are easier and more pleasant to take, which helps if you dislike swallowing pills. But capsules usually fit more active ingredient into one serving, hold up better in heat, cost less per dose, and are easier to make with an accurate label. If you just want to test an ingredient like DHM, capsules are the simpler experiment.

**When should I take hangover gummies?**

Follow the label for your product. Most DHM-based products suggest taking a serving while drinking or before bed, rather than the next morning. Take them with a full glass of water and some food. A gummy taken the morning after is less likely to help than one taken around the time you drink.

**Do PartySmart gummies work?**

PartySmart is a herbal formula from Himalaya, and the company points to its own research showing lower acetaldehyde after drinking. We couldn't find large, independent, peer-reviewed trials of the finished product. It may help some people, and it's usually affordable, but treat it as a modest add-on rather than protection from a hangover.

**Are DHM gummies as good as DHM capsules?**

They can contain the same ingredient, but usually at a lower dose per piece. DHM is bitter and takes up space, so many gummies hold less per serving or ask you to eat several. Check the milligrams of DHM per serving and whether the brand publishes third-party test results. Capsules are typically cheaper per milligram.

**Are hangover gummies safe?**

For most healthy adults taking them as directed, yes, with mild stomach upset being the most common complaint. Herbal blends can interact with some prescription medicines, so ask a pharmacist if you take any. Keep gummies away from children, and away from dogs if they contain xylitol. No gummy lowers your blood alcohol or makes it safe to drive.

**Can you take hangover gummies with melatonin?**

Be careful. Alcohol and melatonin can both make you drowsy, and mixing sleep aids with drinking isn't a good idea. If you want help sleeping after a night out, the safer choice is to stop drinking earlier, drink water, and give your body time before bed. Ask a doctor if you're unsure.
